column3: The Hebrew has both “spoke” and “saying”; BSB gives a single “said.”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew has singular “its flower” and ends with an unnamed “he made”; BSB uses plural “blossoms” and the passive construction “fashioned according to the pattern.”
The Hebrew does not explicitly say “Again,” which BSB supplies.
The Hebrew says to cleanse the Levites; BSB explicitly qualifies this as “ceremonially.”
The Hebrew says to pass a razor over all their flesh; BSB expresses this as shaving their whole bodies.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the Levites” as the recipients of the laying on of hands; BSB uses “them.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew has singular “the head of the bulls” and changes from the Levites laying their hands to a singular command to offer. BSB uses plural “heads” and continues with the Levites as the offerers.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says “from among the sons of Israel”; BSB supplies “the rest” in “from the rest of the Israelites.”
The Hebrew first states that the Levites will enter to serve and then gives the cleansing and presentation commands. BSB places these commands in a preceding “After you have” clause.
The Hebrew repeats “given” twice; BSB expresses the emphasis with “wholly given.”
The Hebrew says “every firstborn” without an explicit word for “male”; BSB makes “male” explicit.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats “the sons of Israel” five times; BSB uses “the Israelites” three times and pronouns for the other two occurrences.
The Hebrew closes by explicitly repeating that the sons of Israel did so to the Levites; BSB incorporates the action into its opening statement and concluding command clause.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew has both “spoke” and “saying”; BSB gives a single “said.”
The Hebrew speaks of an individual entering service in the singular; BSB uses plural “Men.”
The Hebrew describes the individual turning back from the service in the singular; BSB uses plural “they” and “retire.”
The Hebrew continues with singular “he” and repeats the roots for keeping a charge and doing work. BSB uses plural “they” and expresses the duties without those repetitions.
